doc.title: Jay Leonhart interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 15, 1998 [interview 1 of 2]

title: A working week in New York and staying home for his kids
summary: Leonhart describes his in-demand status, staying in New York for his children, and becoming busy on electric bass in the studios as sessions have declined.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: We are filming today in San Diego for the Hamilton College Jazz Archive, and I’m very pleased to have Jay Leonhart with me, who I’m going to say is one of the most in- demand bass players in New York City. Is that right?

Well, I certainly work a lot, and I know that a lot of people like me to play for them so yeah I guess it’s true. I mean I don’t want to be overly humble or anything, but at the same time I think it’s probably true.
What’s a working week like for you in New York City?

Well it’s changed. I’ve been there for thirty years, coming in and out, you know I mean playing, sometimes going on the road a little bit. But a week at its peak involves a lot of recording sessions. I have two kids who are now 23 and 26 as of today, which is February 15, 1998 —

The cameras make you forget. They are 23 and 26. When they were young, I didn’t want to leave them. As they were growing up I didn’t want to be an absentee father at all. I mean for their sake, but mostly for mine. I enjoyed them so much. Because one of the real joys of my life is having these great little kids around. And I just wouldn’t leave. So I tried to entrench myself in whatever music I could in New York City, and nearby. And I was lucky in that I got to be relatively busy as an electric bass player in the studios. And I learned to play it very well, you know a lot of the stuff, I mean I loved it, I loved the instrument, I wasn’t faking. I did enjoy the instrument and still do, I just don’t play it anymore, because I’m 57 now and there’s not a lot of calls for a 57-year-old bass player who plays — doesn’t play half of what the guys are playing now. So you know it’s a very limited position I hold. And so it’s all right, because I work a lot on upright, which is what I started off as anyway, you know, from dust to dust. And really I express myself much more fully on upright bass. And I do a lot of sessions. I don’t do as many now, there just aren’t as many sessions now for some reason.
